DATE: 13 Mar 2025
COUNTRY: Gabon
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Caught in, under or between (excl. dropped objects)
ACTIVITY: Transport - Land
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Driving
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
On Thursday March 13th, 2025, the crew change bus had a road accident. It was 18h30 and after a heavy rain at the 
time of the incident.
The bus driver was driving too close to the road edge to avoid potholes of the road section. While doing so a part of 
the road edge collapsed under the right front bus tire making the bus end its trajectory on the pipelines on the side 
of the road with 28 pax on board.
Immediate action: 
• An alcohol test was performed (negative).
• The TAG removed. 
• Rearranged work because of restricted mobility due to ankle sprain.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Road accident: Bus swerved to avoid potholes and crashed ending up on its side. During emergency exit, one 
passenger twisted his ankle badly and ended with a lost injury.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
The bus had design flaws, and all buses of this type were completely removed from our bus fleet. In addition, the 
procedure for driving on our laterite roads was reviewed.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Work or motion at improper speed
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Work Place Hazards: Inadequate surfaces, floors, walkways or roads
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Work Place Hazards: Storms or acts of nature
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate hazard identification or risk assessment

DATE: 01 May 2025
COUNTRY: Gabon
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Struck by (not dropped object)
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Safe mechanical lifting
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
At around 4am on 1st of May, the two men on the crane were assigned to a new location. The operation involved 
depositing the counterweights. Following a counter-order from the supervisor, they had to carry out a final lift 
before going on to the new location. The spider chains were replaced on the counterweights. As the chains are 
lifted, one of the hooks gets caught in the guide of the counterweight. When the chains come off, they have a spring 
effect. The banksman can't reasonably control three of them and the fourth spins around him with his back lower. 
The spider chain hit the banksman at the back. The IP received pain killer treatment before transferring to hospital 
by chopper. The IP suffered a permanent impairment injury.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The banksman was hit by one of the four hooks on the spider chain.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Poor work planning. 
• Inadequate communication between workers.
• Inadequate execution of the operation. 
• Failure to follow lifting procedures, resulting in risks becoming normalized.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper lifting or loading
PEOPLE (ACTS): Inattention/Lack of Awareness: Improper decision making or lack of judgment
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate hazard identification or risk assessment
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate communication
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Poor leadership/organizational culture

DATE: 18 Aug 2025
COUNTRY: Gabon
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Struck by (not dropped object)
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Work authorization
NARRATIVE:
On 18 August 2025, a team was installing a 6-inch pipe over a 35-metre section between two lines. This pipe was 
also to be used during WO operations. During the operation, the team separated a 6-inch pipe from a 2-inch pipe, 
both of which had previously been tied together with cords. During the lifting phase, the cords were gradually cut 
to separate the two pipes. When the third cord was cut, the tension accumulated in the 6-inch pipe, which was 
bent at the time, was suddenly released. The pipe rebounded and struck an operator's right leg between the ankle 
and knee, causing an open fracture. The supervisor was immediately informed, the control room was alerted, and 
emergency procedures were quickly implemented.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
PI: Right leg open fracture of staff during the connection operation, while lifting a 6-inch pipe and a 2-inch pipe, 
both of which had previously been tied together with ropes on the 18th August 2025.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
All work performed requires a dedicated method statement/JHA. The JHA and PTW are updated for all job 
applicants. Improve the behaviour of the authorities responsible for stopping work at all subcontractors. Review the 
management of the contract.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Tools, Equipment, Materials and Products: Improper use/position of tools/equipment/
materials/products
PEOPLE (ACTS): Inattention/Lack of Awareness: Improper decision making or lack of judgment
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate hazard identification or risk assessment
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate supervision

DATE: 19 Jan 2025
COUNTRY: Gabon
FUNCTION: Construction
CAUSE: Explosion, fire or burns
ACTIVITY: Maintenance, inspection, testing
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Work authorization
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Bypassing safety controls
NARRATIVE:
On January 19, 2025, during restart attempts of the HP-A Gas Compressor following corrective maintenance, 
an unusually loud noise was heard from the exhaust. Seconds later, the fire alarm was triggered, and it was 
observed that the exhaust structure had fallen off. Technicians in the vicinity immediately pressed the compressor’s 
emergency stop button and evacuated the facility. Simultaneously, the emergency response team was activated, and 
the on-scene commander initiated a full facility shutdown using a manual call point near the compressor building. 
Once the source of the loud noise was confirmed to be the HP-A compressor, with the exhaust lying on the ground, 
the area was cordoned off, and an investigation was launched. The compressor was manually shut down, and the 
ESD-1 emergency stop was activated.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
During the starting of gas lift compressor (HP-A), the exhaust pipe of the engine driving the reciprocating 
compressor broke and fell off after several attempts to start it, subsequently activating the fire alarm.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
The crew was not very familiar with the model of engine and didn't know how to react after 1 or 2 attempts to 
restart.
The operating manual was in English not fully understood by the maintenance team.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Deviation unintentional (by individual or group)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Protective Methods: Failure to warn of hazard
PEOPLE (ACTS): Inattention/Lack of Awareness: Improper decision making or lack of judgment
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate hazard identification or risk assessment

DATE: 25 Mar 2025
COUNTRY: Ghana
FUNCTION: Unspecified
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Office, warehouse, accommodation, catering
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
During a heavy rainstorm, two aluminium composite panels (component of the external cladding material for the 
Office building) dislodged and dropped. The two (2) panels, each weighing 9.8kgs and measuring 1.11x1.49ms, 
dropped from about a height of 22.35 meters. The fallen panels were found Infront of the South Wing Power room, 
and the affected area was promptly cordoned off to prevent further hazards. Additionally, multiple panels were 
observed hanging loosely, posing a potential safety risk to occupants and visitors.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
1. Aluminium composite panels not airtight. - Previous investigations revealed that no consideration was given 
to the potential for panels falling during design and installation. Furthermore, subsequent structural integrity 
assessments did not clearly establish the mode of failure and effective mitigation measures to prevent recurrence.
Additionally, in cases where potentially falling aluminium composite panels have been reported, remedial actions to 
remove and reinstall such panels are not promptly executed, despite the high potential impact of a dropped panel.
2. Corrective action process not effectively implemented. - There has been recurring near misses involving dropped 
Aluminium Composite Panels in 2016, 2017, 2018, and 2024. However, corrective actions, such as implementing 
monthly and quarterly drop inspections, have not been sustained.
Furthermore, planned preventive maintenance and other assurance activities that were instituted have not been 
consistently followed and remain areas requiring improvement. For instance, the annual integrity assessment for 
2023 and 2024 were not conducted as planned.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Conduct an integrity inspection and assessment of the external of the entire building to identify any areas of loose 
cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential recurrence of the incident in the short term.
2. Re-institute the conduct of the annual inspection programme of the entire exterior of the building's facade to 
identify any areas of loose cladding and fix them immediately to prevent any potential dropped objects.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Protective Methods: Equipment or materials not secured
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Tools, Equipment, Materials and Products: Inadequate design/specification/management 
of change

PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Work Place Hazards: Storms or acts of nature
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Poor leadership/organizational culture

DATE: 26 Jul 2025
COUNTRY: Nigeria
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Struck by (not dropped object)
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Safe mechanical lifting
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
At about 02:21hrs, while rig crew was picking 4” drill pipe, a single drill pipe was picked from Catwalk to the rig 
floor with Air winch tugger. The IP removed thread protector from the single pipe while another floorman attempted 
to guide the pipe into the mouse hole. The pipe missed the mouse hole, hit the rig floor and also hit the IP on his 
right ear and shoulder. IP was move to Clinic.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
1. Lowering without signal – The air tugger operator lowered the pipe without receiving a stop/lower command, due 
to absence of a dedicated signaller and reliance on previous experience racking 11 stands without one.
2. Obstructed line of sight – The operator was blindsided by the position of already-racked pipes, limiting visibility of 
the mousehole area.
3. IP in fall zone – The injured person was inadvertently in the trajectory of the falling pipe after removing the thread 
protector.
4. Incoherent communication – The floormen recognized the pipe had missed the mousehole but were only able to 
shout warnings, which were not effectively received
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Updating and endorsing the racking SOP.
2. Assigning a dedicated signaller for all pipe-handling operations.
3. Adjusting derrick camera positioning to restore clear line of sight.
4. Reinforcing communication protocols and hazard-zone controls.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Tools, Equipment, Materials and Products: Improper use/position of tools/equipment/
materials/products
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Protective Methods: Failure to warn of hazard
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate communication

DATE: 08 Oct 2025
COUNTRY: Nigeria
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Struck by (not dropped object)
ACTIVITY: Transport - Land
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Driving
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
At about 10:30 hours, a company-owned light vehicle in a security convoy travelling veered off the road and collided 
with an electric pole. The driver and accompanying customer were safely evacuated and transported to the Clinic for 
appropriate medical evaluation / attention.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
1. Driver lost situational awareness and became mentally disengaged (“lost in thought”).
2. Faulty vehicle radio created a quiet environment with no auditory stimulation to help maintain alertness.
3. Vehicle drifted off the road, and driver reaction was delayed.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Effective vehicle safety systems, such as airbags, seatbelts and prompt emergence response minimizes injury 
severity. 
2. Driver to always drive maintaining situational awareness.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Inattention/Lack of Awareness: Lack of attention/distracted by other concerns/stress
DATE: 03 Jun 2025
COUNTRY: Nigeria
FUNCTION: Construction
CAUSE: Exposure electrical
ACTIVITY: Excavation, trenching, ground disturbance
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Energy isolation
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
On 3rd June 2025, at about 2:15pm, during a test digging on a 6" test line right of way, the excavator bucket made 
contact with a buried 11KVA composite electrical cable. The incident resulted in a dent/superficial cut on the cable.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
1. The excavator was used to accelerate exposure of an underground pipeline despite the presence of multiple 
buried utilities.
2. The as-built survey lacked sufficient detail, particularly regarding test line depth and exact routing, leading to 
misinterpretation of subsurface conditions.

DATE: 18 Feb 2025
COUNTRY: Congo
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Production operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Work authorization
NARRATIVE:
A 9 kg metal plate detached from the conveyor railway and fell approximately 6.5–10 m onto the deck below.
No personnel were struck; however, dropped-object energy indicated fatality potential.
The plate was originally installed as a dropped-object prevention measure. Over time it deteriorated and was 
displaced due to a misaligned and stretched conveyor belt, which pushed the plate out of position.
Operations on the starboard conveyor were stopped, the area below was barricaded, and a rope-access inspection 
of similar installations was initiated.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Dropped-object protection plate was not adequately inspected or maintained over time.
• Conveyor belt was poorly fitted/misaligned, creating continuous mechanical load on the plate.
• No inspection programme identified deterioration or displacement risk.Safety-critical equipment (secondary 
retention / guarding) was not recognised as such and therefore not verified.
• Asset integrity management and preventative maintenance were ineffective.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Treat dropped-object prevention devices (guards, covers, retention plates) as safety-critical equipment requiring 
routine inspection.
• Implement a formal inspection and maintenance programme for conveyors and associated guards.
• Correct belt alignment and tension to prevent abnormal loads on structures.
• Periodically survey elevated plant for dropped-object hazards (e.g., DROPS inspections/rope access).
• Ensure barricading/red-zone control beneath overhead equipment during operations where deterioration is 
possible.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Protective Methods: Equipment or materials not secured
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Protective Systems: Inadequate/defective guards or protective barriers
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Tools, Equipment, Materials and Products: Inadequate maintenance/inspection/testing
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate hazard identification or risk assessment

AFRICA OFFSHORE
DATE: 23 Mar 2025
COUNTRY: Equatorial Guinea
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Falls from height
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Safe mechanical lifting
NARRATIVE:
At approximately 06:30, lifting operations were being conducted to move spools from the main deck to the cellar/
sub-cellar deck.
Because no direct lifting path existed, the crew chose to lift the load through a slickline hatch, which constituted 
a complex lift and was not covered by the approved PTW. The crane operator had no line of sight and was 
communicating by radio only.
During lifting, the hook snagged the hatch plate. The rigger, who was standing on the hatch cover to guide the load, 
attempted to stop the lift. The plate dislodged and the rigger fell approximately 6.5 m to the deck below.
The injured person was medevaced with serious injuries. The event had clear fatality potential.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• A complex lifting operation was performed under a PTW that only authorised a standard lift.
• Work scope changed without risk assessment or lift planning.
• Crane operator had no line of sight and communications were unreliable.
• Rigger stood on the hatch cover to guide the load, placing himself in a fall hazard zone.
• The lift was coordinated using voice/radio in a noisy area without clear signalling control.
• Rigger’s certification had expired and supervision was inadequate.
• Unsafe practice had become normalised due to prior similar lifts performed without incident.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Complex lifts require a specific lift plan, risk assessment, and supervision.
• Never route loads through hatches/openings without engineered lifting arrangements.
• Maintain line of sight or use a designated trained signalman with agreed communication protocol.
• Personnel must never stand on removable covers or under suspended loads.
• Verify competency and certification of riggers and lifting personnel.
• Stop work when lift conditions differ from the approved plan.
CAUSAL FACTORS:

PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Work Place Hazards: Congestion, clutter or restricted motion

DATE: 02 Dec 2025
COUNTRY: Gabon
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Struck by (not dropped object)
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Safe mechanical lifting
NARRATIVE:
While parking the starboard (STBD) crane following routine lifting operations, the crane boom was brought down 
into the boom rest abruptly rather than in a controlled manner. This sudden placement generated an unexpected 
impact load on the crane structure, producing a loud bang that was heard in the vicinity of the crane pedestal and 
surrounding areas.
The abrupt motion and resulting impact load may have introduced a shock event into the crane’s hydraulic or 
electrical systems. A process shutdown occurred minutes after this impact, and although the causal link has not yet 
been fully established, the timing suggests the crane event may have contributed to or triggered the shutdown.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Crane boom impacted boom rest heavily.
• Crane incorrectly lowered at the boom rest.
• Lack of experience of Crane Operator.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Mandatory contractor equipment specific training familiarization to be performed onboard and documented with 
new crane operators.
2. Selection of candidates for temporary cover to be formalized with the minimum experience requirement for 
contractor operations
3. New crane operators to be mobilized in advance to come offshore and undergo supervision monitored by the 
facility crane operator for a defined supervision period.
4. Non-destructive testing to be performed at the crane's boom & cradle by 3rd party.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper lifting or loading
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate training/competence
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate supervision

AFRICA OFFSHORE
DATE: 18 Mar 2025
COUNTRY: Mauritania
FUNCTION: Production
CAUSE: Pressure release
ACTIVITY: Maintenance, inspection, testing
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Energy isolation
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
Contractor carrying out repairs on the Scale Inhibitor Injection system, the system was understood to have been 
depressurised. As the contractor started to release an end cap, the cap was projected downwards under pressure. 
The cap went directly downwards into a section of plant close to a walkway. This could have had potential to impact 
personnel.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Failure to properly depressurise closed circuit.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Learning 1. The process for managing valve movements during a leak test in response to a leak was not robust. The 
leak testing procedure was not explicit about how to manage such a situation. Also no bridging document between 
procedure and company Control of Work procedure.
Learning 2. Site team did not verify that the leak test system envelope was fully depressurised. Task fatigue and 
normalisation of the risk were identified resulting in the Permit Authority deciding to de-prioritise some oversight of 
the task.
Learning 3. The potential hazard created using 6Mo tubing and 316 stainless steel fittings at tubing geometries 
outside of manufacturer recommendation was not understood. Knowing this may have influenced decisions around 
controls such as exclusion zones and proving zero energy at the point of system being worked on.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Use of Tools, Equipment, Materials and Products: Servicing of energized equipment/inadequate 
energy isolation
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate work standards/procedures
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate hazard identification or risk assessment

AFRICA OFFSHORE
DATE: 18 Nov 2025
COUNTRY: Namibia
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Safe mechanical lifting
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
NARRATIVE:
Flex Joint strikes handrail creating 2 Dropped Objects. During the removal of the Flex Joint from the Riser Feeding 
Machine (RFM) using the starboard crane, the aft sling of the Flex Joint became hung up on the RFM bucket. As the 
lift continued, the sling suddenly released, causing the Flex Joint to swing unexpectedly.
The uncontrolled movement resulted in the Flex Joint striking and damaging the RFM track and the associated 
emergency-stop device. The Flex Joint then continued its swing path until coming to rest against the starboard-side 
handrail.
The impact dislodged two sections of the handrail, weighing 2.4 kg and 4.6 kg, corresponding to 377 Joules and 722 
Joules of potential energy respectively. Both handrail sections fell approximately 16 metres to the Riser Deck below.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Uncontrolled movement - swing.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Accumulate incident information and ensure proper cause analysis and mitigating measures.
• Set expectations for supervisor 1 to 1 conversations According to: HSE Improvement plan.
• Computer-based training on lift planning.
• Onshore crane and lifting discipline lead and mechanical lifting focal point to discuss systemic standardized 
management of lift plans on vessel.
• Onshore resources to audit the effectiveness of systematic approach to management of lift plan.
• Update procedures for laying out flex joint.
• Ensure OEM compliant cameras for starboard crane are installed.
• The material handling plan for the vessel will need to be MOC from original design - action.
• Inspection and testing required on damaged RFM structure.
CAUSAL FACTORS:
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper position (in the line of fire)
PEOPLE (ACTS): Following Procedures: Improper lifting or loading
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate training/competence
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate work standards/procedures
PROCESS (CONDITIONS): Organizational: Inadequate hazard identification or risk assessment

ASIA/AUSTRALASIA ONSHORE
DATE: 03 Dec 2025
COUNTRY: Australia
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Dropped objects
ACTIVITY: Lifting, crane, rigging, deck operations
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Safe mechanical lifting

riser guide posts with no escape route available. He had earlier climbed onto adjacent baskets and manually guided

against another basket. Emergency response was immediate, and medical evacuation was carried out via search 
and rescue (SAR) helicopter. The investigation identified multiple human, organisational, technical, and task-related 
contributors including lack of hands-free lifting, trainee crane operator without supervision, congested deck layout, 
communication challenges, inadequate planning, and procedural non-compliance.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
Hands-free lifting methods were not used despite being available, exposing personnel to the line of fire. The

into restricted and hazardous positions to open basket covers and guide the BHA manually. No exclusion zone was 
established. Several crew members were new in roles or on the rig, and norms for intervening or stopping unsafe 
work were inconsistent. Organisational follow-up on competence, planning quality, and supervision responsibilities 
was insufficient. These factors created multiple error traps and eliminated critical barriers.

always be established and maintained. Trainee crane operators must only operate under direct mentor supervision 
in accordance with formal competence requirements. Communication expectations with third-party vendors must 
be clear, including language-barrier mitigation. Deck layout planning between logistics and lifting operations must

DATE: 01 Sep 2025
COUNTRY: Norway
FUNCTION: Drilling
CAUSE: Falls from height
ACTIVITY: Construction, commissioning, decommissioning
PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Working at height
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Work authorization
NARRATIVE:
On an offshore drilling rig, on 1 September 2025, personnel and marine crew were installing handrails on top of a 
unit on the main deck. Handrail sections (60–90 kg) were lifted by deck crane to the top of the unit, where an operator 
worked at height to receive and install them, using fall-arrest equipment. The operator initially attached his lanyard 
to the stairs, then to handrail, and later to another section to reach the final corner section. To fit the last section, he 
had to lift and adjust some of the handrail. The locking pins were weakly retained and the chain/carabiner secondary 
securing arrangement did not prevent them from sliding out. The section of the handrail tilted and fell, pulling the 
operator with it. He fell approximately 4.3 m to deck, landing partly on the fallen handrail. The incident resulted in an 
LTI and a dropped object with calculated energy of 2733 J, with assessed potential for a single fatality.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The units were not designed to support safe work at height: the only structurally adequate anchoring points (lifting 
eyes) were located below top deck level and were occupied by lifting bridles during installation, leaving no suitable 
anchor points available. The operator therefore clipped his fall-arrest lanyard to a handrail section that was only 
temporarily secured by a pin, chain, and carabiner. The handrail securing design was inherently weak; on the short 
side of the container, the locking pin had only ~2 mm mechanical engagement and could easily slide out, and the 
chain/carabiner arrangement offered a false sense of security. The installation and commissioning procedure 
mentioned work at height and scaffolding, but did not clearly explain how the handrails should be installed or 
secured, nor the purpose or requirement for scaffold. No scaffold was erected, and the crew changed the intended 
installation sequence, requiring lifting and moving the section used as an anchor. Competence requirements for 
work at height (Norog 113) were not formalised in the competence matrix; several involved personnel lacked formal 
practical WAH training and were unaware of approved anchor point requirements. Project planning and follow-up 
from onshore were insufficient, and the contractor equipment checklist process was not effectively applied.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
Work at height must never rely on temporary structures (such as partially installed handrails) as anchoring points. 
Units that require routine or installation work at height must be designed with suitable, certified anchor points, or 
work must be carried out from properly designed scaffolding or other engineered access solutions. Competence 
requirements for working at height (incl. practical training and anchor-point assessment) must be explicitly built 
into contractor competence matrices and verified before mobilisation. Installation and commissioning procedures 
for vendor packages must clearly describe safe installation methods, including detailed handrail installation 
sequences, locking mechanisms, and when scaffolding is mandatory. Work permits that bundle many high-
risk activities can obscure critical controls; large scopes should be broken into smaller work procedures where 
necessary to ensure hazards and controls are fully understood. A robust equipment and project-follow-up process 
is needed, including use of the correct contractor equipment checklist and clear assignment of onshore and 
offshore responsibility for installation planning and oversight.

PRIMARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Line of fire
SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Working at height
NARRATIVE:
During preparations for installing a 20’’ sealing ring on the platform on 2 July 2025, a technician tested the ring 
for fit before the lift operation. The 7.1 kg ring slipped from the technician’s hands and fell 6.35 meters to the deck 
below, landing approximately two meters from a mechanic who was grinding at deck level. The ring then bounced 
and struck the mechanic on the arm. The mechanic received a first-aid level impact with no observable injury. The 
event had a severe potential for fatality due to the weight and fall height. The ring had been brought into the elevated 
work area earlier than planned, the area was insufficiently barricaded, and the test occurred without notification to 
the crew below. Multiple procedural, communication and barrier-management weaknesses contributed.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The sealing ring was tested earlier than planned, without expanding the barricaded area and without informing 
the crew below. The ring slipped due to inadequate handling conditions (gloves, oily surface). The work area had 
been split into two phases, but equipment was still placed in the elevated area during phase one, creating exposure 
before barriers were in place. Barricading was too small, based on a common but unsafe practice of using minimal 
exclusion zones for “non-loose object” work at height. Communication between team members and between teams 
and was incomplete. The area technician approved only the intent of barricading but did not verify it physically. The 
team lead was cognitively overloaded and new in the role, reducing situational awareness. Stop-work authority was 
not used despite unease among personnel below. The net result was coexistence of workers above and below with 
no effective barrier against dropped objects.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
All work at height must assume potential for falling objects and require full barricading unless a technical barrier 
(e.g., safety net) is installed. Equipment must not be brought into elevated areas before controls are in place. Area 
technicians must physically verify barricades before work starts. Practices that rely on personnel remembering 
not to bring loose items into height work are insufficient; technical and organizational barriers must supplement 
human behaviour. SIMOPS coordination must be strengthened, including explicit identification of all nearby work 
teams and discussion in morning meetings. Communication internally within teams must be improved to ensure 
shared situational awareness. Stop-work authority must be normalised, supported, and used proactively. Project-
wide learning should be shared across platforms to eliminate similar practices elsewhere.

was tensioned with 5 klbs over string weight and rotated manually, but no movement was observed. Based on 
contractors’ instructions, power tongs were partially used due to the absence of a power swivel on site.
During the sixth right-hand turn with a 5 klbs overpull, the 2-7/8" tubing coupling connected to the safety valve backed 
off and fell approximately 21 ft onto the rig floor, then a further 14 ft to the ground. At the same time, the tubing string 
settled approximately 6 ft into the packer. The combined weight of the coupling and safety valve was 36.5 kg.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
1. Uncontrolled rotation using a power tong led to the tubing connection backing off.
2. Thread make-up integrity was not sufficient for rotation under tension.
3. Lack of appropriate equipment (power swivel) resulted in the use of a higher-risk alternative.
4. Dropped-object controls were inadequate, allowing heavy equipment to fall from height.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Management of Change (MoC) must be applied before deviation.
Any deviation from approved procedures, tooling, or operating limits shall be formally reviewed, risk-assessed, and 
approved through the MBPS MoC process prior to execution.
2. Operations must stop when normal operating parameters are exceeded.
When loads, methods, or equipment differ from the original plan, supervisors must stop work and reassess using 
approved Operator procedures and MoC requirements.
3. Contractually required equipment must be available and used as intended.
Operations shall not proceed unless all contract-specified rig equipment is present, functional, and fit for purpose. 
Temporary or partial substitutions are not acceptable.
4. Stop Work Authority (SWA) must be actively exercised and enforced.
All personnel are required to stop work when unsafe conditions exist, including dropped-object exposure, lack of 
secondary retention, or use of non-approved tools or methods.
5. Secondary retention is mandatory for elevated components.
All elevated or moving tools and components shall be secured with secondary retention wherever practicable to 
prevent dropped-object incidents.

NARRATIVE:
On May 20, 2025, a worker was engaged in repositioning a spec blind from the closed to the open position on the 
flare line, in preparation to de-isolate the unit for commissioning activities. During this activity, the worker was 
exposed to a gas/energy release from the down steam side of the isolated gate valve at the open flange pair. Worker 
required rescue from heights and was provided onsite first aid; worker was transported to a local hospital for 
further medical assessment where it was determined worker sustained bruised ribs and a concussion. Worker was 
released from hospital the same day.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
The 10” gate valve used as a single isolation was not fully closed because the chain operator seized due to physical 
interference, giving a false indication that the valve was seated. Pressure verification showed 0 kPag, but this was 
ambiguous because the flare system was under slight vacuum, meaning zero pressure did not confirm positive 
isolation. Oxygen entered the flare piping system through the partially open valve while the flare remained lit, 
creating conditions for ignition. When work was performed on the spectacle blind, this led to a deflagration and an 
uncontrolled release of energy that injured the worker.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. Zero pressure does not equal positive isolation - Pressure indication alone is an insufficient barrier for verifying 
isolation in flare systems, especially where vacuum conditions can exist. 
2. Single isolation is not a robust barrier for breaking containment - Single isolation provides little tolerance for 
hidden failures and should not be relied upon where severe energy release is credible. 
3. Equipment condition and work environment directly shape human decision-making - People act on the cues the 
system gives them; degraded equipment and obstructed layouts can actively mislead competent workers. 
4. Permits and risk classification must reflect real hazard potential - Administrative controls lose credibility when 
they do not reflect the true severity of the hazard.

The fire brigade responded immediately and extinguished the fire using CO₂ and dry powder extinguishers.

WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Cleaning cloths were likely contaminated with a chemical/oily substance capable of self-heating after drying.

• No procedure or segregation process existed for handling contaminated rags.
• Personnel did not recognise the chemical odour as a hazard indicator.

• Treat cleaning rags as potentially oil/chemical contaminated materials.
• Implement segregation and identification of contaminated cloths before laundering.

CAUSE: Explosion, fire or burns

SECONARY LIFE-SAVING RULE:  Hot work
NARRATIVE:
On 27 December at approximately 07:30, cleaning cloths contaminated with cooking oil were washed and dried in 
the laundry.
After drying, the cloths were placed on the floor inside an open bag next to other cloths. Later, all laundry 
ventilation, exhaust, and air-conditioning systems were switched off while the room was unattended.
At approximately 13:15, the cloths began releasing smoke and an incipient fire developed. The steward used a dry 
chemical extinguisher and the fire brigade extinguished the fire.
No injuries or damage occurred, but the event had serious fire potential.
WHAT WENT WRONG:
• Oil-contaminated cloths were washed and dried without special handling precautions.
• Hot cloths were stored in a pile/bag, allowing heat accumulation and self-heating.
• Laundry ventilation and cooling were shut down while the cloths were unattended.
• No procedure existed for segregation, cooling, or disposal of oily rags.
• Hazard of spontaneous combustion from oil-soaked rags was not recognised.
CORRECTIVE ACTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
• Segregate oil/grease contaminated cloths before laundering.
• Do not place recently dried cloths in piles, bags, or enclosed areas - allow them to cool individually in a 
ventilated metal container or spread out.
• Maintain ventilation/exhaust until materials have cooled.
• Implement procedures for handling and disposal of contaminated rags.
• Train personnel on spontaneous combustion risks (oils, hydrocarbons, solvents).
• Provide fire-resistant rag bins and designated storage areas.
